title: Taiwan Railway's Lunch Boxes Earn a Record NT$876 Million
summaryZh: 台鐵便當去年營收8.76億元創新高，排骨最熱賣

summaryEn: Taiwan Railway's boxed meals earned a record NT$876 million last year, with pork chop the clear favourite.
paragraphs: Taiwan Railway Corp's boxed meals, a familiar part of train travel on the island, brought in record revenue of NT$876 million (US$26.89 million) last year, an increase of 9.07 percent on the previous year.

The company sold 9.42 million boxes, roughly 25,800 a day. Although that fell short of the 10.54 million sold in 2019, the year with the highest sales volume, each box now earns more, pushing revenue to an all-time high.

The railway began selling boxed meals in 1949. Early versions mainly contained a pork chop with a braised egg and dried tofu or tofu skin, and the pork chop remains its signature dish, accounting for 7.18 million boxes last year. Chicken leg was a distant second at 560,000, while braised pork belly and fish options were added over time.

Taipei Station was by far the biggest outlet, selling 2.65 million boxes, ahead of Xinzuoying Station in Kaohsiung with 800,000 and Banqiao Station in New Taipei City with 680,000. The meals are prepared by six catering divisions in Taipei, Keelung's Cidu, Taichung, Kaohsiung, Hualien and Taitung, with the Taipei division producing the most, about 3.5 million.
Looking ahead, the company says it will continue to raise quality, introduce seasonal specialities and use local ingredients to attract customers and keep sales strong.
On many trains in Taiwan, people eat a lunch box. The Taiwan Railway has sold these boxes since 1949. Many people buy one at the station before their trip.
Last year, the railway made a record amount of money from lunch boxes: NT$876 million. It sold 9.42 million boxes. That is about 25,800 boxes every day.
The most popular box has a pork chop. People bought 7.18 million of them. Chicken leg was second, with 560,000.
Taipei Station sold the most boxes: 2.65 million. Next were stations in Kaohsiung and New Taipei City.
The railway wants to make the food even better. It plans new boxes for each season, with food from local farms.
Taiwan Railway's famous lunch boxes are making more money than ever. The company says sales reached a record NT$876 million (about US$26.9 million) last year, up 9.07 percent from the year before.

It sold 9.42 million boxes, or about 25,800 a day. That number is still lower than in 2019, when it sold 10.54 million boxes, but each box now earns more, so the total income was the highest in its history.

Taipei Station was the busiest seller, with 2.65 million boxes, followed by Xinzuoying Station in Kaohsiung (800,000) and Banqiao Station in New Taipei City (680,000). The boxes are made in six kitchens around the island.

Taiwan Railway Corp's humble boxed meal has become a surprisingly lucrative business. Revenue hit a record NT$876 million (US$26.89 million) last year, a 9.07 percent rise on the year before.

Volume tells a slightly different story. The 9.42 million boxes sold, around 25,800 a day, still trail the 2019 peak of 10.54 million. In other words, the railway is earning more from each meal, which has lifted overall revenue to an unprecedented level despite lower sales.

Boxed meals have been on sale since 1949, when a typical box held a pork chop alongside a braised egg and dried tofu or tofu skin. Seven decades on, the pork chop remains the undisputed bestseller, with 7.18 million sold last year, dwarfing the runner-up, chicken leg, at 560,000. Braised pork belly and fish have since broadened the menu.

Demand is concentrated in the north: Taipei Station alone sold 2.65 million boxes, well ahead of Kaohsiung's Xinzuoying Station (800,000) and New Taipei City's Banqiao Station (680,000). Production is spread across six catering divisions, from Keelung's Cidu to Taitung, with Taipei turning out the largest share, about 3.5 million meals.
To sustain this momentum, the company intends to keep refining quality, roll out seasonal specialities and source more local ingredients.

For generations of travellers, the railway lunch box has been an integral part of a train journey in Taiwan, and it is now proving more commercially successful than ever. Taiwan Railway Corp reports that boxed meal revenue reached an unprecedented NT$876 million (US$26.89 million) last year, representing growth of 9.07 percent year on year.

Intriguingly, this record was achieved without a record in volume. Sales of 9.42 million boxes, equivalent to approximately 25,800 per day, remain below the 2019 peak of 10.54 million. The figures therefore suggest that average revenue per meal has risen considerably, offsetting the decline in the number of units sold.

First introduced in 1949, the meals originally consisted mainly of a pork chop accompanied by a braised egg and dried tofu or tofu skin. The pork chop has retained its dominance, accounting for 7.18 million boxes, while the chicken leg option trailed far behind at 560,000. The range has gradually diversified to include braised pork belly and fish.

Geographically, consumption is heavily concentrated: Taipei Station sold 2.65 million boxes, compared with 800,000 at Xinzuoying in Kaohsiung and 680,000 at Banqiao in New Taipei City. Six regional catering divisions share production, with Taipei's the largest contributor.

To maintain this momentum, the operator plans further quality improvements, seasonal specialities and a greater reliance on local ingredients, a strategy designed to attract new customers while retaining loyal ones.

use.ex: The old bridge is no longer in use.

using.ex: Using a map helped us find the hotel.

versions.en: forms of something that differ slightly
versions.ex: The book comes in two versions.

volume.en: the amount or number of something

wants.ex: She wants a quiet place to study.

well.ex: Keep well back from the edge.

were.ex: The shops were closed on Sunday.

will.en: used to talk about the future
will.ex: The new bridge will open next year.

words.en: in other words: saying it another way
words.ex: Choose your words carefully in an interview.
